claims.claim: The location of GIP-1 and GIP-2 clusters closely match the dgMTOC regions defined by EBP-2 comets.
claims.source: GIP-1 precisely localized to the site from which EBP-2 comets originated (Figure 2C) and quantification of the distribution and location of GIP-1 and GIP-2 clusters showed that their location closely match the dgMTOC regions defined by EBP-2 comets (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: No GIP-1 or GIP-2 clusters were found in the cell body, axon, or posterior dendrite during their outgrowth.
claims.source: These γ-TuRC clusters are specific to the outgrowing anterior dendrite since no GIP-1 or GIP-2 clusters were found in the cell body, axon, or posterior dendrite during their outgrowth (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), consistent with the lack of an apparent MTOC in these structures.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged but absent near the tip of mature dendrites.
claims.source: Furthermore, growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) but absent near the tip of mature dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: The dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
claims.source: Furthermore, growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) but absent near the tip of mature dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the temporal localization of GIP-2.

claims.claim: GIP-2 localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron.
claims.source: Significantly, GIP-2 also localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further supporting a more general role for the dgMTOC in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The dgMTOC has a more general role in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
claims.source: Significantly, GIP-2 also localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further supporting a more general role for the dgMTOC in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of GIP-2 localization in multiple neuron types.

claims.claim: Expression of ZIF-1 in the developing PVD lineage led to a dramatic reduction of punctate GFP::GIP-1 signal in ~80% of outgrowing PVD anterior dendrites.
claims.source: Expression of ZIF-1 in the developing PVD lineage led to a dramatic reduction of punctate GFP::GIP-1 signal in ~80% of outgrowing PVD anterior dendrites (GIP-1PVD(-), Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: GIP-1PVD(-) animals showed a striking reversal of anterior dendrite MT polarity leading to plus-end-out orientation in both outgrowing and mature dendrites in about half of the animals.
claims.source: We then examined EBP-2 comets in GIP-1PVD(-) animals, which revealed a striking reversal of anterior dendrite MT polarity leading to plus-end-out orientation in both outgrowing and mature dendrites in about half of the animals (Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: In GIP-1PVD(-) animals, many dendritic comets originated from the cell body.
claims.source: Unlike in wild-type (wt) animals where the majority of EBP-2 comets were generated by the dgMTOC, in GIP-1PVD(-) animals, many dendritic comets originated from the cell body (Figure 2F and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2F and Video 3.

claims.claim: γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC.
claims.source: These results indicate that γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC and that the dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects observed upon GIP-1 depletion.

claims.claim: The dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
claims.source: These results indicate that γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC and that the dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects observed upon GIP-1 depletion.

claims.claim: The highest MT density was found ~2–4 µm from the dendritic tip, consistent with the presence of an MTOC in this region.
claims.source: In our EM series, numerous short, staggered MTs were observed with their ends unambiguously identified. Consistent with our EBP-2 and TBA-1, the highest MT density was found ~2–4 µm from the dendritic tip, consistent with the presence of an MTOC in this region (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EM reconstruction data in Figure 3A–C.

claims.claim: Serial EM reconstruction showed no evidence of a centriole or Golgi outpost in the dgMTOC area.
claims.source: Serial EM reconstruction showed no evidence of a centriole or Golgi outpost in the dgMTOC area.
claims.evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: Numerous clear- and dense-core vesicles were found in between the MT arrays in the dgMTOC area.
claims.source: Instead, numerous clear- and dense-core vesicles were found in between the MT arrays (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Clusters of clear-core vesicles were found in the region with the highest MT numbers suggesting that GIP-1 and GIP-2 might localize to these vesicles to function in the dgMTOC.
claims.source: In particular, clusters of clear-core vesicles (Figure 3B, white) were found in the region with the highest MT numbers suggesting that GIP-1 and GIP-2 might localize to these vesicles to function in the dgMTOC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of vesicles and high MT density.

claims.claim: The synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3 was not enriched in the dendritic growth cone region.
claims.source: Synaptic vesicles are the most abundant clear-core vesicles in neurons; however, the synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3, which robustly localized to the axon (Maniar et al., 2012), was not enriched in the dendritic growth cone region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The early/medial Golgi cisternae markers RER-1 and AMAN-2/alpha-mannosidase 2 were only present in the cell body but not in the growth cone.
claims.source: Consistent with our EM results, the early/medial Golgi cisternae markers RER-1 (Sato et al., 2011) and AMAN-2/alpha-mannosidase 2, the latter of which localizes to Golgi outpost MTOCs at mature dendrite branch sites in D. melanogaster (Ori-McKenney et al., 2012), were only present in the cell body but not in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The late-Golgi compartment marker RAB-6.2 was enriched in the growth cone in a localization pattern similar to that of γ-TuRC.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the late-Golgi compartment marker RAB-6.2 (Zhang et al., 2012) was enriched in the growth cone in a localization pattern similar to that of γ-TuRC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The recycling endosome marker RAB-11.1 co-localized and moved together with RAB-6.2-labeled vesicles in the growth cone.
claims.source: Therefore, we further examined recycling endosomes and found that the recycling endosome marker RAB-11.1 co-localized and moved together with RAB-6.2-labeled vesicles in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: RAB-11.1 showed striking co-localization with GIP-2.
claims.source: Notably, RAB-11.1 showed striking co-localization with GIP-2 (Figure 3D), with 81.7 ± 3.5% (SEM, n = 11) of RAB-11.1 fluorescence overlapping with GIP-2 and 80.6 ± 5.2% (SEM, n = 11) reciprocal GIP-2 fluorescence overlapping with RAB-11.1 in the growth cone (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: RAB-11.1 displayed a nearly identical movement pattern to that of GIP-2, with both proteins moving together in the growth cone.
claims.source: Time-lapse recordings revealed that RAB-11.1 displayed a nearly identical movement pattern to that of GIP-2, with both proteins moving together in the growth cone (Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: A frame-to-frame analysis of RAB-11.1 and GIP-2 distribution showed high correlation in the growth cone.
claims.source: A frame-to-frame analysis of RAB-11.1 and GIP-2 distribution showed high correlation in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), but no correlation in the cell body (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G; Costes et al., 2004; Manders et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claims.claim: Co-localization and co-trafficking of RAB11.1 and GIP-2 suggest that Rab11-endosomes may be at the core of the dgMTOC.
claims.source: Co-localization and co-trafficking of RAB11.1 and GIP-2 suggest that Rab11-endosomes may be at the core of the dgMTOC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and co-trafficking data.

claims.claim: Rab11-associated endosomes and Rab11 itself have been found to influence the MT organization of mitotic spindles.
claims.source: Interestingly, Rab11-associated endosomes and even Rab11 itself have been found to influence the MT organization of mitotic spindles (Hehnly and Doxsey, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals.
claims.source: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) (Ren et al., 1998) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals (Figure 3H and J, n = 28, Figure 3—source data 1) and a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, n = 28).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3H and J.

claims.claim: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) caused a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals.
claims.source: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) (Ren et al., 1998) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals (Figure 3H and J, n = 28, Figure 3—source data 1) and a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, n = 28).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: 20% of Cre expressing worms displayed a loss of GIP-2 puncta in the dendritic growth cone with mislocalization of GIP-2 as either multiple dim puncta dispersed within the cell body (12%) or along the dendrite shaft (7%).
claims.source: 20% of Cre expressing worms displayed a loss of GIP-2 puncta in the dendritic growth cone with mislocalization of GIP-2 as either multiple dim puncta dispersed within the cell body (12%, Figure 3J,i1 and i2 in Figure 3I, n = 41) or along the dendrite shaft (7%, i3 in Figure 3I), suggesting transportation or clustering defects.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3J and imaging in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: γ-TuRC localization to RAB-11.1-positive endosomes in the growth cone underlies the dgMTOC, which generates short plus-end-out MTs in the distal growth cone and dynamic minus-end-out MTs that populate the growing dendrite.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that γ-TuRC localization to RAB-11.1-positive endosomes in the growth cone underlies the dgMTOC, which generates short plus-end-out MTs in the distal growth cone and dynamic minus-end-out MTs that populate the growing dendrite.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on γ-TuRC and RAB-11.1 localization and function.

claims.claim: The mature PVD anterior dendrite loses minus-end-out MTs and gains plus-end-out MTs in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants.
claims.source: We previously showed that the mature PVD anterior dendrite loses minus-end-out MTs and gains plus-end-out MTs in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants (Taylor et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: unc-116(e2310) mutants showed a large decrease in the percentage of minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrite shaft during outgrowth.
claims.source: Consistent with the MT polarity defect in mature PVD dendrites, unc-116(e2310) mutants showed a large decrease in the percentage of minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrite shaft during outgrowth (wt: 93.8 ± 2.7% (SEM, n = 11); unc-116(e2310): 21.4 ± 10.4% (SEM, n = 12); Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: The reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth.
claims.source: Additionally, the reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth (using the unc-86 promoter), but not rescued by expressing unc-116(+) after anterior dendrite outgrowth (using a ser-2 promoter), suggesting that UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
claims.source: Additionally, the reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth (using the unc-86 promoter), but not rescued by expressing unc-116(+) after anterior dendrite outgrowth (using a ser-2 promoter), suggesting that UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: In unc-116 mutants, the vast majority of MTs originated from the cell body and were plus-end-out throughout the anterior dendrite.
claims.source: In striking contrast to wt, unc-116 mutants lacked a convergence of plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in the outgrowing dendritic growth cone. Instead, the vast majority of MTs originated from the cell body and were plus-end-out throughout the anterior dendrite (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D and Video 4), raising the possibility that the dgMTOC is inactive or mislocalized in unc-116 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: In unc-116 mutants, many EBP-2 comets emanated from a single region within the cell body indicating a putative MTOC.
claims.source: By tracing the origin of EBP-2 comets over time in unc-116 mutants, we frequently observed that many EBP-2 comets emanated from a single region within the cell body indicating a putative MTOC (Figure 4C and Video 5) – a stark contrast to the lack of a point-of-origin for EBP-2 comets in GIP-1PVD(-) animals (Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4C and Video 5.

claims.claim: GIP-2 was largely absent from the outgrowing dendritic growth cone and instead formed a cluster within the cell body in 64% of unc-116 mutants.
claims.source: Unlike in wt, GIP-2 was largely absent from the outgrowing dendritic growth cone and instead formed a cluster within the cell body in 64% of unc-116 mutants (n = 45, Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: RAB-11.1 formed a cluster within the cell body rather than in the growth cone region in 71% of unc-116 mutants.
claims.source: RAB-11.1 also formed a cluster within the cell body rather than in the growth cone region in 71% of unc-116 mutants (n = 28, Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, Figure 4—source data 1), providing further support that Rab11 endosomes are a component of the dgMTOC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The kinesin-1 motor is required for localizing the dgMTOC to the outgrowing dendritic growth cone.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that the kinesin-1 motor is required for localizing the dgMTOC to the outgrowing dendritic growth cone.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mislocalization of the dgMTOC in unc-116 mutants.

claims.claim: The location of the dgMTOC instructs MT polarity.
claims.source: Furthermore, while depletion of GIP-1 in PVD showed that the dgMTOC is required to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs, this unc-116 mutant phenotype suggests that the location of the dgMTOC instructs MT polarity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between dgMTOC location and MT polarity.

claims.claim: GIP-2 fluorescence undergoes processive movements toward the distal tip.
claims.source: Time-lapse analyses of GIP-2 cluster movement showed that GIP-2 fluorescence undergoes processive movements toward the distal tip with several features.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: GIP-2 movements are largely unidirectional toward the distal dendrite tip.
claims.source: First, GIP-2 movements are largely unidirectional toward the distal dendrite tip, which is evident in kymograph analysis (f1 in Figure 4F), GIP-2 cluster localization at different time points (left and right panels of f2 in Figure 4F) and quantification of the anterior displacement of the GIP-2 cluster (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4K.

claims.claim: GIP-2 localization alternates between a tight cluster and a broader cluster with more dispersed puncta.
claims.source: Second, GIP-2 localization alternates between a tight cluster and a broader cluster with more dispersed puncta (middle and right panels of f2 in Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: GIP-2 movements are interspersed by pauses.
claims.source: Third, the movements are interspersed by pauses (middle panel of f2 in Figure 4F), which is also evident by the alternating slopes and plateaus in GIP-2 moving distance analyses (black trace in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Most GIP-2 exists in a bright cluster during pauses, while the fluorescence is dispersed into multiple smaller puncta during the mobile phase.
claims.source: Most GIP-2 exists in a bright cluster during pauses, while the fluorescence is dispersed into multiple smaller puncta during the mobile phase (f2 in Figure 4F and Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4F and Video 6.

claims.claim: GIP-2 moves in a saltatory manner, with cycles of aggregation and dispersal, toward the distal dendritic tip.
claims.source: These results indicate that GIP-2 moves in a saltatory manner, with cycles of aggregation and dispersal, toward the distal dendritic tip.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed dynamics of GIP-2 movement.

claims.claim: unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants showed largely reduced movement or dispersal of GIP-2 clusters.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants showed largely reduced movement or dispersal of GIP-2 clusters (Figure 4G and J–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 7, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4G and J–L.

claims.claim: UNC-116/kinesin-1 moves GIP-2 containing endosomes in the outgrowing dendrite.
claims.source: These analyses suggest that UNC-116/kinesin-1 moves GIP-2 containing endosomes in the outgrowing dendrite.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reduced GIP-2 movement in unc-116 mutants.

claims.claim: The individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34).
claims.source: Interestingly, we noticed that unlike minus-end-out MTs which transitioned rapidly between polymerization and depolymerization (Figures 1C and D and a3 in Figure 5A, triangle-shaped peaks in kymographs, Figure 5—source data 1), the individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34) (a2 in Figure 5A, plateaus, Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
claims.source: Interestingly, we noticed that unlike minus-end-out MTs which transitioned rapidly between polymerization and depolymerization (Figures 1C and D and a3 in Figure 5A, triangle-shaped peaks in kymographs, Figure 5—source data 1), the individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34) (a2 in Figure 5A, plateaus, Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed pausing behavior of plus-end-out MTs.

claims.claim: The distal plus-end-out MTs originating from the cell body in unc-116 mutants also paused in the tip of the dendrite and showed similar pause frequency and time as wt animals.
claims.source: We note that the distal plus-end-out MTs originating from the cell body in unc-116 mutants also paused in the tip of the dendrite and showed similar pause frequency and time as wt animals (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the pausing of plus-end-out MTs in the growth cone is independent of UNC-116 function.

results.result: A dendritic growth cone MTOC (dgMTOC) exists in C. elegans PVD neurons that generates minus-end-out microtubules toward the cell body and plus-end-out microtubules toward the growth cone tip. This was demonstrated through EBP-2 comet tracking and TBA-1 dynamics showing MT nucleation from a discrete region near the dendrite tip, with high MT density 2-4 μm from the tip.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C27-C40 provide converging evidence from multiple independent approaches (EBP-2 comet tracking, TBA-1 dynamics, EM reconstruction) demonstrating the existence and activity of the dgMTOC. The quantification of comet frequency (0.44 comets/s), directionality measurements, and MT density profiles provide strong quantitative support. The dgMTOC is specific to the anterior dendrite and absent from axon and posterior dendrite.

results.result: A similar dgMTOC structure exists in Drosophila melanogaster Class I sensory neurons, suggesting evolutionary conservation of this mechanism for establishing dendritic MT polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C35, and C140 demonstrate the dgMTOC in Drosophila through EB1::GFP imaging showing bidirectional MT polymerization from the growth cone region. This cross-species validation strengthens the generality of the finding, though the Drosophila data is less extensively characterized than the C. elegans data.

results.result: The γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) components GIP-1 and GIP-2 localize to the dgMTOC region and track with the advancing growth cone during dendrite outgrowth. This localization is specific to the anterior dendrite during development and is absent from mature dendrites, axons, and posterior dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C50 demonstrate γ-TuRC localization through endogenous tagging and live imaging. The co-localization of GIP-1/GIP-2 with EBP-2 comet origins (C44-C45) and quantification of their spatial distribution (C45) provide strong evidence. The temporal pattern (present during outgrowth, absent in mature dendrites, C47) and observation in multiple neuron types (C49) support the developmental role.

results.result: Conditional knockdown of GIP-1 in PVD neurons causes loss of the dgMTOC and reversal of MT polarity from minus-end-out to plus-end-out in dendrites, demonstrating that γ-TuRC is essential for establishing dendritic MT polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 provide loss-of-function evidence through ZIF-1/ZF-mediated GIP-1 degradation. The dramatic reduction of GIP-1 puncta (~80%, C51) correlates with MT polarity reversal (~50%, C52), with comets now originating from the cell body (C53). The incomplete penetrance is acknowledged and attributed to partial knockdown, which is reasonable given the conditional approach.

results.result: Serial section electron microscopy reveals the highest MT density 2-4 μm from the dendritic tip, with no centriole or Golgi outpost present. Instead, numerous clear-core and dense-core vesicles are found in the dgMTOC region.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 provide ultrastructural validation of the dgMTOC through EM reconstruction. The MT density distribution (C56) matches the functional data from live imaging. The absence of canonical MTOC structures (C57) and presence of vesicles (C58-C59) are clearly documented, though the inference that GIP-1/GIP-2 localize to these vesicles (C59) requires additional validation.

results.result: RAB-11.1-positive recycling endosomes co-localize and co-traffic with γ-TuRC (GIP-2) in the dgMTOC region, with 81.7% of RAB-11.1 overlapping with GIP-2 and high frame-to-frame correlation in the growth cone but not cell body.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 systematically identify the vesicular component of the dgMTOC through marker analysis. The exclusion of synaptic vesicles (C60) and early/medial Golgi markers (C61), combined with positive identification of late-Golgi/recycling endosome markers (C62-C63) and quantitative co-localization analysis (C64-C66), provide strong evidence that RAB-11.1 endosomes are the structural basis of the dgMTOC.

results.result: Interference with RAB-11.1 function through dominant-negative expression or conditional knockout causes loss or mislocalization of GIP-2 from the growth cone and MT polarity defects, suggesting RAB-11.1 influences dgMTOC organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C135-C136 demonstrate RAB-11.1 requirement through two independent approaches: dominant-negative (35% loss of GIP-2, 10% MT polarity defects) and conditional knockout (20% GIP-2 mislocalization). The modest penetrance is acknowledged and may reflect incomplete disruption or redundancy. The correlation between GIP-2 mislocalization and MT polarity defects supports the functional connection.

results.result: UNC-116/kinesin-1 is required for localizing the dgMTOC to the dendritic growth cone during early development. In unc-116 mutants, the dgMTOC mislocalizes to the cell body, resulting in loss of minus-end-out MTs (93.8% to 21.4%) and plus-end-out MTs throughout the dendrite originating from the cell body.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C82 demonstrate kinesin-1's role through mutant analysis and temporal rescue experiments. The dramatic MT polarity reversal (C74), mislocalization of both GIP-2 (64%, C79) and RAB-11.1 (71%, C80) to the cell body, and temporal requirement during early outgrowth (C75-C76) provide strong evidence. The observation that dgMTOC location correlates with MT polarity (C82) supports the instructive model.

results.result: GIP-2-positive endosomes undergo saltatory movements toward the dendritic tip, characterized by cycles of aggregation and dispersal interspersed with pauses. These movements are largely abolished in unc-116 mutants, indicating kinesin-1 transports the dgMTOC components.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 characterize dgMTOC dynamics through time-lapse imaging and quantitative analysis. The description of unidirectional movement (C84), alternating cluster states (C85), and pauses (C86-C87) is well-documented. The dramatic reduction in movement and dispersal in unc-116 mutants (C89) provides strong evidence for kinesin-1-mediated transport.

results.result: Plus-end-out MTs in the growth cone are transiently stabilized (pausing for 10.34 ± 0.85 s), and RAB-11.1 endosome movements preferentially occur during these pause periods. This stabilization is independent of UNC-116 function and provides tracks for kinesin-1-mediated dgMTOC transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C102 establish the mechanism of selective transport through detailed MT dynamics analysis. The quantification of pause duration (C91), demonstration that pausing is UNC-116-independent (C93-C94), correlation between endosome movement and MT pausing (C98-C99), and positive correlation between movement distance and pause time (C99) provide strong mechanistic insight. The model is well-supported by the data.

results.result: DHC-1/dynein localizes to the dgMTOC and is required for clustering γ-TuRC-positive endosomes. In dhc-1 mutants, GIP-2 exhibits repeated dispersal without forming stable clusters, and ~50% show complete MT polarity reversal with another ~20% showing mixed polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C116 demonstrate dynein's role through mutant analysis and localization studies. The multiple classes of GIP-2 mislocalization (C104-C106), failure to maintain cluster integrity (C108-C109), co-localization and co-movement with RAB-11.1 (C110-C111), and MT polarity defects (C113-C114) provide strong evidence. The model that dynein re-clusters dispersed endosomes (C115-C116) is well-supported.

results.result: The dgMTOC is a γ-TuRC-based, endosome-associated structure that advances with the growing dendrite through coordinated kinesin-1 and dynein activity. It is required to establish initial minus-end-out MT polarity during development, and its location is instructive for MT polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The evidence from γ-TuRC localization (C119), motor protein requirements (C120), and instructive role demonstrated by ectopic minus-end-out MTs when dgMTOC is mislocalized (C121) strongly support this integrative conclusion. This represents the central finding of the manuscript.

results.result: The minus-end-out MT orientation initially established by the dgMTOC is likely maintained by additional mechanisms in mature dendrites, including cortical anchoring through Ankyrin-CRMP complexes and other MT orientation-guiding mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 acknowledge that dgMTOC function is developmental and that maintenance requires additional mechanisms. The observation that dgMTOC is absent in mature dendrites (C47) while minus-end-out MTs persist supports this conclusion. The citation of cortical anchoring mechanisms (C124) provides a plausible maintenance mechanism, though this is not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: The dgMTOC establishes minus-end-out MTs in primary dendrites during early outgrowth, distinct from Patronin-mediated minus-end growth that acts in terminal branches at later developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 distinguish the dgMTOC mechanism from other known mechanisms through temporal and spatial considerations. The observation that dgMTOC acts during primary dendrite outgrowth (C128) before branching, while Patronin acts in terminal branches (C126), and that patronin mutants still develop initial minus-end-out MTs (C127) support distinct mechanisms operating at different developmental stages.

results.result: RAB-11.1-marked endosomes provide a scaffold for γ-TuRC assembly to form the dgMTOC, similar to how Rab11-endosomes deliver spindle material to centrosomes in mitotic cells, suggesting Rab11-endosomes may be a general source of MTOC material.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C134 propose a structural model based on co-localization, co-trafficking, and co-mislocalization data (C130-C131). The parallel to mitotic spindle organization (C133) provides conceptual support. While the scaffold model (C132) is a reasonable inference from the data, direct biochemical evidence for γ-TuRC assembly on RAB-11.1 endosomes is not provided.

results.result: RAB-11.1 may interact with dynein to localize and cluster the dgMTOC, based on similarity of phenotypes between RAB-11.1 knockout and dynein mutants, and known interactions between Rab11 and dynein during mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 propose a molecular interaction based on phenotypic similarity (dispersed GIP-2 puncta in both rab-11.1 and dhc-1 mutants) and literature precedent (C137). However, no direct evidence for RAB-11.1-dynein interaction in this context is provided. The model is plausible but requires biochemical validation through co-immunoprecipitation or other direct interaction assays.

results.result: The dgMTOC is a widespread and conserved mechanism for establishing minus-end-out MT populations in primary dendrites, with evidence in both C. elegans and Drosophila, and multiple dgMTOCs can exist in different dendritic processes of the same neuron.
results.evaluation: Claims C139, C141-C142 extend the findings to propose generality. The observation in multiple C. elegans neurons (PVD, DA9) and Drosophila (C34, C140), and the presence of dgMTOCs in both primary dendrites of Drosophila neurons (C141) support conservation and flexibility of the mechanism. However, the Drosophila data is less extensively characterized.

results.result: A dgMTOC could establish the minus-end-out MT population during dendrite outgrowth in mammalian neurons, which contain mixed MT polarity. Different cell types may tune MT dynamics programs to achieve different ratios of plus-end-out to minus-end-out MTs.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 are speculative extrapolations to mammalian systems. While C143 states established knowledge about mammalian dendritic MT polarity, C144-C145 are explicitly speculative ("We imagine," "We speculate"). No mammalian data is presented. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not supported by data in this manuscript.

results.result: Background claims establishing that axons contain exclusively plus-end-out MTs while dendrites contain predominantly minus-end-out MTs, that MT polarity is functionally important for trafficking, and that MTOCs organize cellular MT arrays.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C12-C16 establish background knowledge through citations to prior work. These are well-established facts in the field and appropriately cited. They provide necessary context for understanding the significance of the dgMTOC discovery.

results.result: Prior work has proposed multiple mechanisms for generating minus-end-out MTs in dendrites, including Golgi outposts, endosome-based nucleation at branch sites, ciliary base nucleation, motor-based MT sliding, MT steering, and minus-end growth, but the mechanism establishing initial polarity during development remained unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25 comprehensively review prior mechanisms through appropriate citations. The authors accurately represent prior work and identify the gap (initial establishment during development) that their work addresses. The distinction between maintenance mechanisms and establishment mechanisms is important for framing the contribution.

results.result: The dgMTOC is present throughout anterior dendrite outgrowth, appearing as soon as the dendrite emerges and persisting until maturity, suggesting a developmental role in establishing MT organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C31, C47-C48 establish the temporal pattern of dgMTOC presence through imaging at different developmental stages. The observation that GIP-2 is present during outgrowth but absent in mature dendrites (C47) supports a developmental role (C48), though this inference could be strengthened with more detailed time-course analysis.

results.result: Rab11-endosomes and dynein have established roles in organizing MTs in mitotic spindles and concentrating organelles near MTOCs in non-neuronal cells, providing precedent for their roles in the dgMTOC.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C103, C133 cite relevant prior work establishing roles for Rab11-endosomes and dynein in MT organization in other cellular contexts. These citations appropriately support the plausibility of similar roles in the dgMTOC and provide conceptual framework for interpreting the findings.
